metaDescription: Five Hisense dehumidifiers from 25 to 60 pints compared by pump, cold-room limits and drain setup, so you can size one for a bedroom or a large basement.
expertTake: The Hisense 60-pint with the built-in pump is the pick for a large or cool basement because it keeps working down to 38F and lifts water to a distant drain. The 35-pint is the value pick for a bedroom or mid-size room. If your problem is a single closet, skip the compressor range entirely.
introParagraphs: A compressor dehumidifier is only as useful as the conditions it can work in. Cold rooms, awkward drains and noisy fans decide whether a unit earns its floor space, long before a headline pint number does.

This range moves up in clear steps, which makes the decision about the room and the drain rather than about brand loyalty. Reading the details on temperature limits, pump lift and control layout shows which step fits which space.

products.name: Hisense 60-Pint Dehumidifier with Built-In Pump, 4,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
This is the Hisense to buy when the space is large, cool and has no convenient drain. A built-in pump with a quick-connect hose lifts water away from the machine, so the unit can sit in a corner of a below-grade basement and discharge to a utility sink or a standpipe. The quick-connect fitting is a small detail that matters: you can unplug the hose to move the machine without a mess.

Its 60-pint rating is the highest in the lineup, ten pints above the 50-pint models and a clear step over the 35-pint. It also operates in air as cold as 38F, which is well below the roughly 65F where many compressor units start losing output. That cold tolerance makes it the better choice for an unheated basement or a garage workshop that sees a few cold months.

In ownership terms, the programmable 24-hour on and off timer lets you run it during cheaper electric hours, and a bucket-full indicator warns you if you switch the pump off and use the tank. Wash the filter monthly, test the pump at the start of each humid season and keep the hose from kinking behind the cabinet. If the room is under about 3,000 square feet, a 50-pint will do the job at lower cost.
products.bestFor: Large, cool basements where no floor drain is nearby.

products.name: Hisense 50-Pint Lift-Up Portable Dehumidifier with Built-In Pump

specList.label: Best space
specList.value: Large basement without a floor drain

products.description:
The lift-up model gives you a pump on a 50-pint machine, which is a sweet spot for a lot of houses. It drains continuously through an included hose without you lifting a bucket, so it suits a basement where the drain is on another level. The three operating modes include Auto and Continuous, and there are three fan speeds, so you can trade noise against drying speed.

Against the 60-pint, it gives up ten pints of rated capacity and about the same coverage class, which for a moderately damp basement is rarely noticeable. Against the plain 50-pint without a pump, it adds drain flexibility at a higher cost. The lift-up label refers to the pump hose arrangement that lets the unit empty upward.

Ownership comes down to the pump and the filter. Check the hose end is secured, rinse the filter every few weeks and watch for a pump that runs dry when the bucket is removed. Because a pump hides how much water the machine is making, glance at the discharge once in a while to confirm it is still flowing.
products.bestFor: Moderately damp basements with an uphill or distant drain.

products.name: Hisense 50-Pint Portable Dehumidifier, 4,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The plain 50-pint is the straightforward large-room Hisense. It uses the same 4,500 square foot rating as the pump version, with three modes and three fan speeds, and it leaves out the pump. A hose lets it drain continuously by gravity, and the bucket is there if you prefer to empty by hand.

Compared with the 35-pint, it adds fifteen pints of rated capacity, which is the extra margin a damp open floor wants. It also lists low-temperature operation, so a cool basement does not shut it down the way a basic unit might. Where it differs from the pumped 50-pint is the drain: you need a floor drain at or below the machine.

It is the economical way to get a large-room Hisense, as long as the plumbing cooperates. Keep the intake clear of walls and stored boxes, wash the filter on schedule and verify the setpoint with a separate hygrometer rather than trusting the built-in reading alone.

products.name: Hisense 35-Pint Compact Dehumidifier, 3,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
The compact 35-pint is built around portability. A slide-out bucket makes emptying easy and a built-in handle makes it simple to carry from room to room. Coverage is listed at up to 3,000 square feet, and the product page calls it energy efficient and quiet.

It sits in the middle of the Hisense ladder, above the 25-pint and well below the 50-pint models. For a bedroom, a bathroom or a mid-size basement with a steady problem, that is a good balance of size and output. It is not the unit for a wet unfinished basement, where it would run constantly.

Ownership is simple: wash the filter, empty the bucket and move it with the handle when you need to. If you can set up a hose, do it, because a full bucket stops the unit. For a second room, the 25-pint is a lighter, cheaper companion.

products.name: Hisense 25-Pint Compact Portable Dehumidifier, 1,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The 25-pint is the entry Hisense and the simplest to operate. It uses straightforward manual controls, and continuous drain is set by pressing the minus button until CO shows on the display. It lists low-temperature operation, which is unusual for a unit at this size.

Its coverage figure of 1,500 square feet is half that of the 35-pint, so it fits a bedroom, a bathroom or a small utility room. In a larger basement it would run nonstop and still fall behind. That is the cost of the small cabinet and the low profile.

It is the easiest to carry, store and live with. Use the hose connection if you cannot empty the bucket daily, and keep the room closed so the unit is only working on a small volume of air.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Pick the step for the room
buyingCriteria.explanation: Hisense sells 25, 35, 50 and 60 pint steps, rated for roughly 1,500, 3,000, 4,500 and 4,500 square feet. A bedroom or bathroom suits the 25-pint, a mid-size room suits the 35-pint and a basement suits a 50 or 60. A musty smell or visible condensation usually means you should go one step up from what the square footage says. Also remember that both 4,500 square foot models share that label even though one removes ten more pints, so the extra capacity is headroom for a stubborn problem rather than extra floor area.

A compressor unit chills a coil, and below about 65F the coil frosts and output falls. The 60-pint lists operation down to 38F and several others list low-temperature operation. If your basement or garage is cold for months, that limit matters more than the pint rating. A unit running at its cold limit still removes less water than it does in a warm room, so size up a step when the space stays near the bottom of its range, and consider a small space heater for a very cold room.

The 60-pint and the 50-pint lift-up have built-in pumps with an included hose, while the plain 50, 35 and 25 depend on gravity. A pump costs more and adds a part, but it solves a drain that sits above the machine. Check the vertical distance to your drain before choosing. Also confirm the hose length reaches the discharge point without a loop that traps water, since a sagging hose can slow the flow and make a pump work harder than it should.

The 50-pint models offer three modes and three fan speeds, and the 60-pint adds a 24-hour timer. The 25-pint keeps things to manual buttons. More modes help if you run the unit on a schedule, but a plain dial is easier for someone who just wants it to work.

The 35-pint has a slide-out bucket and a carry handle, and the 25-pint is the lightest. A big machine is heavy enough that you will avoid moving it, so a handle matters if you share a unit between rooms. Choose the smaller unit if you intend to carry it. Empty the bucket before you lift it, since a full 35-pint bucket adds several pounds of sloshing water, and use the handle rather than the bucket recess when moving the cabinet.

A 50 or 60 pint unit can fill a bucket in hours in a wet room. The 60-pint has a bucket-full indicator and a pump, which removes the chore. Be honest about whether you will empty daily, because a unit that is full is an unplugged unit. If you travel often or use the space as a second home, favor a pump model or a hose into a floor drain so the machine keeps running while you are away.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity ladder
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how the 25, 35, 50 and 60 pint steps map to room sizes and listed coverage. A clear ladder helps buyers size correctly. We treated the figures as spec sheet claims, not measurements.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cold-room tolerance
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated low-temperature limits, especially the 38F figure on the 60-pint. Cool basements are the common failure case. Units without a stated limit scored lower for cold rooms.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drain flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the pumps on the 60-pint and the 50-pint lift-up against the gravity-only models. A pump with a quick-connect hose scored highest. Simple hose ports scored well for simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls and convenience
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed modes, fan speeds, the timer and the bucket-full indicator. More features help schedule-driven users, while manual buttons suit simple use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative price tiers, from the 35-pint at a lower tier to the 60-pint at the top. The best value is the smallest unit that actually handles the room.

cards.label: Pump (60-Pint, 50-Pint Lift-Up)
cards.text: Lifts water to a distant drain and uses a hose that can be unplugged for moving. It adds a component and a cost. It suits basements where the drain is on another level.

cards.label: Gravity (50-Pint, 35-Pint, 25-Pint)
cards.text: Simpler and cheaper with nothing to fail. It needs a downhill path or manual emptying. It suits spaces with a floor drain.

howToChoose.note: Pick the pump when the drain is uphill, and gravity when a floor drain is close.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: At least 50 pints for a moderately damp basement, a drain that works with gravity or a pump and a stated cold limit. Leave room around the intake and keep the unit off the wettest part of the floor.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 60-Pint with Pump is the best for cool, large spaces, the 50-Pint Lift-Up suits awkward drains and the plain 50-Pint is the value choice with a floor drain.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The room is cool, the drain is uphill or you want a timer. The 60-Pint and 50-Pint Lift-Up earn their cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The room is a bedroom or bathroom. The 25-Pint or 35-Pint handle it for less.

maintenance.why: A clogged filter chokes airflow and invites coil frost. Rinse and dry it fully before reinstalling.
Standing water grows slime and odor. Mild soap and a rinse prevent it.
A pump that sits idle can stick. Run a cycle and watch the discharge.
Dust cuts heat transfer and efficiency. Unplug the unit before opening.
Kinks and sediment stop flow and cause overflow. Confirm it drains freely.

faq.q: Which Hisense size do I need?
faq.a: A bedroom or bathroom suits the 25-pint, a mid-size room suits the 35-pint and a basement suits the 50 or 60. If the space smells musty or shows condensation, go one step up so the unit cycles off.
Yes when the drain is above the machine or on another level. A floor drain nearby makes the plain 50-pint a simpler choice with one less part.

faq.q: Do Hisense units work in a cold basement?
faq.a: The 60-pint lists operation down to 38F and several others list low-temperature operation. Most compressor units lose output near 65F, so a stated limit is worth reading.

faq.q: What does a higher pint number really mean?
faq.a: It describes how much water a unit can pull under a stated test, and the condition matters as much as the number. Coverage and room dampness decide whether a bigger unit is needed. A bigger unit also draws more power, so it is only worth choosing when the extra capacity will actually be used.
Compressor models commonly last 5 to 10 years. Cleaning the filter and coil and avoiding an undersized unit are the main levers.

Between 40 and 50 percent is the usual target. Above 60 percent invites mold, and below 30 percent feels dry. Confirm with a separate hygrometer. Built-in humidistats can read a few points off, so a second reading in the far corner of the room is worth the small cost.
